subject: Critical Thinking
title: Depolarization: Bridging Divided Minds
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Depolarization: Bridging Divided Minds.

hook.text: Americans overestimate how extreme the other side is by a factor of 2.

buildup.text: Depolarization research shows that most people are more moderate than their online representatives suggest.

discovery.text: The 'More in Common' project found that the 'exhausted majority' – 67% of people – are tired of polarization but feel.

twist.text: Media and algorithms amplify the extremes. The moderate middle doesn't go viral. Outrage does. The signal is distorted.

climax.text: Solutions: encounter the real out-group, focus on shared concerns, and reduce the perception gap through contact.

punchline.text: We share more ground than conflict suggests, but trust is what makes it visible.

quiz.question: What is the 'perception gap' in polarization?
options: People overestimate how extreme the opposing side is compared to reality
There's a gap in how news is perceived

details.summary: Depolarization strategies aim to reduce ideological division by finding common ground, humanizing opponents, and restructuring conversations away from binary thinking. They address the psychological roots of polarization, not just its symptoms.
details.whyItMatters: Political and social polarization threatens democratic institutions, personal relationships, and collective problem-solving.
takeaways: Exposure to moderate opposing views reduces polarization
Humanizing the other side is more effective than debating issues
Structural changes to information environments can help

faq.question: What psychological approaches have been shown to reduce polarization?
faq.answer: Perspective-taking exercises, inter-group contact with shared goals, exposure to moderate opposing voices, and conversations focused on personal stories rather than positions.

faq.question: Why can exposure to extreme opposing views sometimes increase polarization?
faq.answer: Extreme views confirm negative stereotypes of the other side, triggering defensive reactions and reinforcing group identity rather than encouraging open-mindedness.
